title: How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks (rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, MFA, IP blacklisting, monitoring, short-lived tokens)?
shortTitle: How do you secure sensitive endpoints from brute-force attacks
keyPoints: Defence in depth: no single control stops brute force; layer rate limiting, lockout, CAPTCHA, MFA, and monitoring.
Rate limiting caps attempts per time window per account and per IP at the API gateway.
Account lockout temporarily disables after repeated failures, with progressive delays to avoid DoS on legitimate users.
CAPTCHA challenges automated scripts after a few failed attempts without annoying legitimate users on first login.
MFA is the strongest single control: a guessed password is useless without the second factor.
Monitoring and alerting turn silent attacks into visible ones by tracking failure rates and lockout spikes.
Short-lived tokens limit the blast radius if a credential is eventually guessed or stolen.

s1_definition.oneliner: Stop brute force with layers: rate-limit attempts, lock accounts after repeated failures, challenge with CAPTCHA, require MFA so a password alone is useless, blacklist abusive IPs, monitor and alert on patterns, and keep tokens short-lived.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Rate limiting** – Cap attempts per time window per account and per IP, enforced at the API gateway.
- **Account lockout** – Temporarily disable an account after too many failed logins; use progressive delays to avoid enabling DoS.
- **CAPTCHA** – A human-verification challenge shown after a few failures, blunting automated scripts.
- **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** – Require a second proof (OTP, hardware key) so a password alone is useless.
- **IP blacklisting** – Block known-abusive sources, statically from threat intelligence or dynamically on threshold breach.
- **Monitoring** – Track failed-login rates and alert on spikes to catch credential stuffing across many accounts.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine thieves trying thousands of PINs at a National Bank of India ATM. Rate limiting lets the machine accept only a few tries per minute. Account lockout swallows the card after three wrong PINs. CAPTCHA asks a question only a human can answer. MFA requires both the card and a one-time code sent to Rajesh's phone. IP blacklisting bans a specific thief who keeps coming back. Monitoring is the security camera that calls the guard when it sees a pattern.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Brute Force Defence Layers:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Attacker: 10,000 credential-stuffing         │
  │  attempts per minute from botnet              │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                     │
  ┌──────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Layer 1: Rate Limit (gateway)               │
  │  Per IP: 20/min, Per account: 5/min          │
  │  -> 95% of attempts blocked with 429         │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                     │ ~500 attempts pass
  ┌──────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Layer 2: Account Lockout + CAPTCHA          │
  │  After 3 failures: CAPTCHA required          │
  │  After 5 failures: 15-min progressive delay  │
  │  -> ~50 attempts pass CAPTCHA                │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                     │ ~50 attempts with correct password
  ┌──────────────────▼───────────────────────────┐
  │  Layer 3: MFA                                │
  │  Correct password but no OTP -> BLOCKED      │
  │  -> 0 successful logins without 2nd factor   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Defending sensitive endpoints from brute force requires layers, because each control covers a different gap. Rate limiting caps the velocity of attempts per account and per IP. Account lockout with progressive delays stops single-account guessing without enabling DoS. CAPTCHA blocks automated scripts after a few failures. Multi-factor authentication is the strongest single control because a guessed password is useless without the second factor.

IP blacklisting blocks persistent abusive sources, monitoring detects credential stuffing across many accounts that per-account lockout misses, and short-lived tokens limit the blast radius of any eventual compromise. At National Bank of India, thousands of rapid attempts hit Rajesh's account. The gateway rate-limited and dynamically blacklisted the IP, the account locked after repeated failures with progressive delays, CAPTCHA was demanded after three, and even a correct password failed without the MFA code.

The senior nuances matter: hash passwords with BCrypt so offline guessing is expensive, return generic failure messages so you never reveal whether the username or password was wrong, apply the same throttling to password-reset and OTP endpoints which are common blind spots, and combine weak signals like unusual geography, new device, and rising failures into a risk score that triggers step-up authentication.

Remember one sentence: stop brute force with layered defence: rate-limit per account and IP, progressive lockout, CAPTCHA after failures, MFA so a password alone is worthless, monitoring for failure spikes, and short-lived tokens to minimize blast radius.
